HEADLINE: Ten million testing kits
TEXT:
Pathology | Donations from billionaire Andrew Forrest's Minderoo Foundation have secured 10 million COVID-19 test kits and pathology equipment for use across Australia.

The kits give the nation's largest pathology providers, Sonic Healthcare and Healius, greater testing capacity.

The equipment will be supplied by China's Beijing Genomics Institute, US life sciences firm Thermo Fisher Scientific and Swiss laboratory instruments provider Tecan Group.

The government will enter into supply contracts with private pathology providers for the 13 BGI and 14 Tecan lab systems to expand testing.

More than 500,000 COVID-19 tests have been completed in Australia. Adding 10 million tests equates to an almost 20-fold increase.

The iron ore billionaire and his wife, Nicola, recently donated $520 million to their Minderoo charitable foundation, bringing their donations to more than $2 billion. They are also helping fund a drug trial to combat COVID-19.

The Fortescue Metals founder and chairman is a long-time advocate for better relations with China and has praised its people for helping Australia fight the virus, including China's ambassador to Australia Cheng Jingye.

The government said the increased capability would enable Australia to expand the testing criteria.

Healius boss Malcolm Parmenter said the pathology group will ramp up COVID-19 testing from next week.

Health Minister Greg Hunt thanked the Forrests for the donation.

HEADLINE: Westpac warns against immigration cuts
TEXT:
Westpac chief economist Bill Evans has warned the Morrison government to resist any temptation to cut immigration in response to a spike in the jobless rate.

Instead, he said Australia should be willing to go even further into debt and sacrifice its AAA credit rating if that was needed to achieve sweeping tax reforms and drive economic growth out of the COVID-19 shock.

Immigration policy is expected to come under pressure, with Westpac predicting the unemployment rate to reach about 9 per cent by the end of June, even with the JobKeeper package in place. Westpac forecasts unemployment to stay above 6 per cent in 2021 and 2022 and for Australia's debt levels to reach 35 per cent of GDP after the stimulus packages cease, a level that has already put it at risk of a credit rating downgrade.

Mr Evans said Australia had responded to high unemployment in the early 1990s by slashing immigration and there was a danger in pursuing a similar strategy.

He said productivity and population growth were drivers of economic growth.

"We get productivity growth with better targeted taxes and less regulation, and we get strong population growth with immigration," he said.

Separate to the economic growth argument, Mr Evans told a conference of farm leaders and investors yesterday that changes to immigration policy posed a major threat to the agriculture sector, which relies heavily on overseas workers.

The government would need to slash inflated unemployment benefits if it wanted to get people back to work in the recovery from COVID-19.

The government has said the doubling of the JobSeeker allowance is temporary.

Mr Evans said in a situation where there was a lot of spare capacity in the younger and lower-skilled segment of the labour market, it would be "very difficult for businesses to pay the sort of wages that will make it competitive for people to leave unemployment benefits".

The recessions of the early 1980s and 1990s provided the impetus for key reforms and COVID-19 presented another such opportunity.

"We can't lose sight of the fact that we need reform, we need growth," he said.

"If it means that our debt blows out further and we have to take a rating downgrade, then I'd be prepared to take that in order to take advantage of this shock to try and boost growth in the economy.

"If we don't, we'll be condemned to this 6 to 7 per cent unemployment rate, high degrees of spare capacity in the labour market, very weak wages growth and very disappointing [economic] growth."

Mr Evans said the national cabinet provided a platform for progress on introducing a broad-based land tax and repeal of "terribly inefficient" state-based payroll and transaction taxes.

The land tax and an increase in the GST could fund reform of state-based taxes and income tax cuts.

Key pointsEconomist Bill Evans says productivity and population are drivers of growth.

Spending and tax reform will help Australia emerge stronger after COVID-19.

HEADLINE: Hunt queries Wuhan origin claim
TEXT:
Health Minister Greg Hunt has contradicted his own government's insistence that the coronavirus pandemic originated in a Wuhan "wet market" during a joint press conference with a senior Chinese diplomat and mining magnate Andrew Forrest.

As relations between Canberra and Beijing plumb new depths, Mr Hunt said it was "not the government's position" that it started in a wildlife wet market, inadvertently providing a boost to Chinese propaganda which denies culpability for unleashing the deadly pandemic on the globe.

Mr Hunt's comments were made at a press conference to announce Mr Forrest had brokered the delivery of 10 million COVID-19 testing kits from China.

China's Victorian consul-general Long Zhou - whose attendance was a surprise to senior ministers - hailed the deal as "another testimony of the friendship and the co-operation between our two countries and the two peoples".

But Mr Zhou also rejected criticism China had bungled its response to the outbreak, saying his government had shared information in an "open, transparent and responsible manner" and co-operated with the World Health Organisation.

During a question to Mr Forrest over whether he agreed with the Australian government's view the virus began in a Wuhan wet market, Mr Hunt stepped in and said, "That's not the government's position".

"We know that it was spread early - that's a universal view," he said.

"We have said that it is most likely that it came from what are called zoonotic sources - so from animal to human. As to the original source, that's not been determined.

"We do know, and all have agreed, that it was early spread within a wet market and we've expressed our views on that."

Mr Hunt's response contradicts his own comment in an ABC TV interview on April 14, when he said, "There is a very real likelihood that this disease arose from a wet market in Wuhan".

And it is at odds with Prime Minister Scott Morrison, who last week said "the virus began in China, in Wuhan, that's, I think that is well understood".

Mr Morrison has taken a hardline against the ongoing operation globally of wildlife wet markets - where wild exotic animals are sold for human consumption - because of the risk of transmitting viruses to humans.

One reason the government has been determined in wanting an independent international review is to counter Beijing's narrative China was not the source of the virus.

As part of the blame game, China has floated a conspiracy theory the virus was brought into the country by a US soldier, while President Donald Trump said US officials were investigating if the virus escaped from a Wuhan research lab.

Mr Hunt's office did not elaborate why the minister said it was not the government's position the virus begun in a Wuhan wet market.

Mr Zhou's attendance at the press conference was being seen by senior government sources as an indication China wanted to take the heat out of the latest spat between Canberra and Beijing, triggered this week when China's ambassador to Australia warned Mr Morrison's pursuit of an inquiry could lead to a Chinese consumer boycott.

Mr Morrison also moved to de-escalate tensions. While firm he would continue to advocate for an international inquiry, Mr Morrison opted against firing back at Beijing in the face of personal attacks on him from state-run media.

"There is not going to be agreement on all of those issues all the time and I think the key to Australia's relationship is just being consistent. And we are consistent on all of the measures on where there has been some potential," he said.

Mr Forrest yesterday urged the government to shelve its push for an inquiry until after the US presidential election in November, given Mr Trump's determination to blame China for the virus.

"A COVID-19 inquiry worldwide is commonsense but it is not to be a Chinese inquiry. That would make it instantly political," Mr Forrest told the ABC.

"I also don't see what the rush is all about. If this is held after the US presidential election, then let's just say there is not going to be a political dog in this fight."

In the tit-for-tat, the Chinese embassy defended itself against the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade's complaint it had breached diplomatic protocol by releasing details of a phone call between departmental secretary Frances Adamson and Chinese ambassador Cheng Jingye.

Ms Adamson spoke to Mr Cheng following his warning to The Australian Financial Review that Australian goods and services could suffer a Chinese consumer boycott if the government persisted in its demands for an inquiry.

"The embassy of China doesn't play petty tricks, this is not our tradition. But if others do, we have to reciprocate," the embassy said in a statement.

HEADLINE: Ho's Crown exit deals Blackstone into game
TEXT:
The dramatic end to Lawrence Ho's investment in Crown Resorts has opened the door for US investment giant Blackstone to dust off previously abandoned plans to split Crown's valuable property assets into a separate vehicle worth as much as $4 billion.

Crown confirmed yesterday that Blackstone had paid $552 million for the 9.99 per cent stake held by Mr Ho's Melco Resorts.

It is less than 12 months since Mr Ho spent $880 million to buy that stake from former business partner and close personal friend James Packer in June 2019.

But while Mr Ho had agreed to buy a second 9.99 per cent stake from Mr Packer, and declared he wanted to own even more of Australia's biggest casino company, the coronavirus has ended his ambitions of becoming a major player in Australia's casino sector and left him nursing a huge loss.

Mr Ho's exit also spares him the ordeal of being scrutinised by a NSW gaming inquiry, which was looking into his purchase of Crown shares and the Sydney casino licence held by the company.

It leaves Mr Packer with a 36 per cent stake in Crown and pinning his hope on the success of his Barangaroo casino in Sydney, which is due to be completed in December.

All 41 casinos in Macau were shut in February as COVID-19 swept through China. Melco's two casino resorts re-opened in late March, but Macau's border remains effectively closed to tourists, with a 14-day mandatory quarantine period enforced.

Gaming revenue in Macau plunged almost 80 per cent in March and Hong Kong-based Bernstein analyst Vitaly Umansky said he expected a 95 per cent fall in April.

Mr Ho abandoned his plans to proceed with the purchase of a second tranche of Crown shares in February, and said later that month Melco's ownership of its existing stake in Crown was under review given the turmoil in Macau.

Mr Umansky, who pointed out Mr Ho's losses were even greater in US dollar terms given the Australian dollar has weakened substantially in the last year, said it was no surprise that Melco had chosen to "move on, get the cash in the door and focus on Macau".

Melco said in a statement to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange that it had sold out "to facilitate its core operations [including operations in Macau, the Philippines and Cyprus] and to strengthen the balance sheet of Melco Resorts during the recent COVID-19 pandemic".

Several local investors speculated that Mr Ho may have also been deterred from investing in Crown due to the intense spotlight placed on the deal through a public inquiry by the NSW government's Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority (ILGA).

But sources in the Melco camp said liquidity, not scrutiny, was Melco's only concern.

A spokesman for the ILGA inquiry said it "will be giving consideration to [Melco's] announcement and any adjustments that may be necessary regarding the ongoing work of the inquiry", which was deferred earlier this month due to COVID-19.

It is understood Mr Ho made a courtesy call to Mr Packer, who is in the US, before the deal was confirmed by Crown yesterday morning.

While Melco's sale would appear to further dampen Mr Packer's hopes of reducing his stake in Crown to diversify his interests, investors cheered Blackstone's investment given its reputation and its strong existing interest in casino properties.

Crown shares climbed 10.9 per cent to close at $9.54, a four-week high.

"Having an interested investor that has a view on the value of the property is probably a good thing," one major shareholder said.

"You've got to look past the next six months with COVID-19 and that's obviously what these guys are prepared to do."

Blackstone, which manages $US538 billion ($824 billion), declined to comment. The deal was led by the firm's head of real estate acquisitions for Asia, Alan Miyasaki.

But Wilson Asset Management portfolio manager John Ayoub said the US investment giant understood the value of casino properties, which are typically located in high-traffic hotspots and seen by governments as crucial infrastructure.

While the shutdown of Crown due to COVID-19 health measures had seen its share price fall 27 per cent since the market's recent peak on February 20, Mr Ayoub said prices of privately held property have not fallen nearly as sharply, and Blackstone may have spotted a bargain.

"Blackstone has got form. They've done this several times over the years and they're quite shrewd," he said.

In January, the Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust paid $US4.6 billion for the underlying property of two casino hotels in Las Vegas, the MGM Grand and the Mandalay Bay.

The trust also holds the underlying property of the Bellagio in Las Vegas, purchased last year for $US4.25 billion, and The Cosmopolitan, where it also owns the operating rights.

Mr Ayoub said Blackstone may see a similar chance to split off Crown's property portfolio.

HEADLINE: Macquarie, Brookfield couple up for Virgin
TEXT:
Exclusive | Street Talk | Macquarie Group and Canadian powerhouse Brookfield have teamed up again and are jointly running numbers on a bid for Virgin Australia.

Two years after both firms made hundreds of millions of dollars co-investing in Western Australian oil company Quadrant Energy, Macquarie and Brookfield are expected to spearhead a consortium with room for others to join the bid.

Stephen Cook, Macquarie's global head of transportation finance, is thought to be heavily involved. He has spent years stitching up aircraft leasing deals for Macquarie clients and oversees Macquarie AirFinance. Deloitte, Virgin Australia's administrator, holds the airline's first creditors' meeting today. Street Talk p13, Companies p14
